Enterprise B2B · Multi-persona · Workflow Design · Global Scale

When a 240-year-old trading firm needed to stop losing incidents in spreadsheets

ED&F Man Capital Markets operates across 50+ countries in high-stakes commodity trading. Incidents — safety, compliance, security, operational — were being reported, bounced back, and forgotten across disconnected systems. We built the module that finally closed the loop.

My role
Lead UX Designer
Timeline
8 months
Team
2 PM, 4 Eng, 1 Data
Impact
↓ 64% bounce-back
Client: ED&F Man Capital Markets · Volcafe Division · Internal enterprise tooling · Web
01Design
strategy

Start with the problem,
not the solution

The brief from the client was simple: "Build a form to replace the email chain." Six weeks of research later, the problem statement had changed completely. This wasn't a form problem. It was a communication gap between two personas who had never shared a system — and a workflow with no defined closure condition.

I defined four design goals that would govern every decision through the project.

01
Reduce the bounce-back loop
The core failure: submitters guessing at requirements, reviewers rejecting with vague feedback. Every design decision had to attack this cycle.
02
Serve two personas without forcing compromise
Admins need control and audit trails. End users need speed and clarity. Both are non-negotiable. Separate contexts, shared data.
03
Define a formal closure condition
The old system had no concept of "done." An incident could exist indefinitely. Every incident needed a traceable path from report to closure.
04
Make the invisible visible
Status, ownership, and overdue actions existed only in people's heads or private spreadsheets. Surface them — for everyone, in real time.
02Profile &
personas

Two people.
One incident. Almost no shared context.

After 14 contextual interviews and a support ticket audit, two primary personas emerged — with fundamentally different mental models of what "a complete incident" meant.

Persona A — The Submitter
Pomilla S.
Operations Manager · Coffee Division · United Kingdom
Reports 4–6 incidents per quarter, always alongside her primary job
No visibility into what the Risk Team needs after she submits
Interprets "Business Impact" differently every time — no shared definition
Doesn't understand why she's asked for Root Cause before her incident is even approved
Checks incident status by replying to the original email thread
Submit it right, first time. Don't want to revisit it.
Every "Insufficient Information" rejection costs 40+ minutes and creates anxiety about compliance.
Persona B — The Risk Reviewer
Ravi G.
Risk Owner · Global Risk Team · India
Manages 30–50 active incidents across multiple business units simultaneously
Needs complete, audit-ready data — regulatory exposure if anything is missing
Responsible for escalating unresolved incidents to compliance officers
Spends ~2 hours daily chasing status updates via email
Tracks overdue action items in a personal spreadsheet nobody else can see
Complete incident data, traceable to closure. No gaps when regulators ask.
Vague submissions mean rejection emails. Rejection emails mean delays. Delays mean compliance risk.
"The same form. Two completely different ideas of what it was for."
— Core research insight, week 3
03Field
studies

Go where the work
actually happens

Six weeks of field research across three divisions (UK, US, India). The most important decision: observe before asking. Surveys would have confirmed assumptions. Observation surfaced the reality.

◎
Contextual Inquiry
Shadowed 6 incident submitters during live reporting sessions. Observed what they skipped, what confused them, and what they googled while filling the form.
Output → Behavioural patterns, confusion hotspots
◈
Stakeholder Interviews
14 semi-structured interviews with submitters, risk reviewers, compliance officers, and engineering leads. Mapped conflicting definitions of "complete."
Output → Mental model map, terminology conflicts
◆
Support Ticket Analysis
Analysed 6 months of rejection emails and support tickets. Tagged by reason, frequency, and persona. Found that 78% of rejections used the phrase "please add more detail" with no specifics.
Output → Quantified pain points, bounce-back taxonomy
◇
Competitive Audit
Reviewed 5 comparable enterprise incident management tools (ServiceNow, Jira Service Desk, Resolver, LogicGate, Origami). Benchmarked form guidance patterns and multi-step workflows.
Output → Pattern library, gap analysis
◉
Card Sorting
Online card sort with 18 participants to validate the IA. Key finding: users expected RCA and Action Plan to live inside the incident — not as separate menu items.
Output → IA validation, navigation model
◐
Usability Testing (3 rounds)
Tested 3 prototype variants with 8 users each. Round 1: concept validation. Round 2: form flow and comments sidebar. Round 3: end-to-end lifecycle with both personas.
Output → Interaction refinements, task completion rates
04Data
gathered

What the research
actually told us

Key findings from synthesis. Not every insight made it into the design — these are the ones that changed a decision.

64%
Incidents bounced back on first submission
The bounce-back rate was 64% at baseline. Not because submitters were careless — because the form gave no guidance on what "complete" meant in context.
78%
Rejection emails with no actionable feedback
"Please add more detail" appeared in 78% of bounce-back emails. Submitters couldn't act on it. Reviewers didn't have a structured way to communicate specifics.
27
Average overdue action items at any given time
No single person had visibility into all overdue actions. Ravi tracked his in a spreadsheet; others tracked nothing. Incidents died quietly.
2 hrs
Daily time spent by Risk Reviewers on status emails
Two hours of every reviewer's day went to manual status chasing. This was entirely a visibility problem — the data existed, but it was locked in email threads.
"I don't know if my incident was rejected or just lost. There's no difference from where I sit."
— Pomilla S., Operations Manager, during contextual inquiry session
05Task
analysis

What each persona
actually does, step by step

Task analysis decomposed the end-to-end incident workflow into atomic actions. This revealed where the two personas' paths diverged — and where they needed to share information without realising it.

Submitter — Pomilla
  • 1
    Click Create Incident
    Identifies event as reportable. Locates the reporting tool and clicks Create Incident.
  • 2
    Fill Details
    Business unit, location, type, description, cost, risk owner.
  • 3
    Fill Root Cause Analysis
    Adds RCA entries with responsible parties and timelines.
  • 4
    Fill Action Plan
    Assigns actions to team members and sets due dates.
  • 5
    Submit Incident
    Submits the completed incident for review.
  • 6
    Reviewer accepts/rejects
    Waits for the reviewer to accept or reject the incident.
Reviewer — Ravi
  • 1
    Receive new incident notification
    Gets email or checks dashboard. Opens incident from list.
    Pain: No prioritisation. All incidents look the same.
  • 2
    Review incident details
    Checks all required fields. Verifies business unit, impact, cost accuracy.
  • 3
    Flag incomplete fields
    Sends rejection email. Describes what's missing.
    Pain: No structured way to specify which field. Email is ambiguous.
  • 4
    Approve incident + monitor RCA
    Approves when complete. Tracks RCA completion separately.
  • 5
    Track action item progress
    Monitors due dates. Chases overdue items manually.
    Pain: Spreadsheet-based tracking invisible to others.
  • 6
    Verify effectiveness & close
    Confirms actions were completed. Formally closes the incident.

09Final
design
All screens — shipped product
From dashboard to closure
Incidents list — notification strip surfaces status changes inline. "View Comments" CTA appears only on Insufficient Information rows. Filter controls: date, status, type.
Report new incident — Step 1
Progressive sub-wizard. Inline guidance on every field. Left sidebar shows where you are.
Editing with Risk Team comments
The contextual comments panel. Reviewers annotate specific fields — submitters see exactly what to fix.
Step 2 — Root Cause Analysis
RCA entries as a table. "+ Add RCA" keeps the form light until needed. Same layout pattern as Action Plan.
Step 3 — Action Plan (form)
Individual action item form. Title, business impact, due date, completion notes. Two text areas for actions required.
Step 3 — Action Plan (table)
"Submit Incident" becomes active once at least one action item exists. Prevents empty closures.
Incident detail — RCA tab
Post-submission view. Three tabs: Incident Details, Root Cause Analysis, Action Plans. Full audit trail in one place.
Dashboard — collapsed sidebar maximises content. KPI strip: Total Incidents, Open, Closed, Overdue Actions. The "27 overdue actions" problem made visible and ownable for the first time.
↓ 64%
Bounce-back rate — incidents approved on first submission
↓ 85%
Overdue action items — from 27 average to 4 within first quarter
1,400+
Users across 14 countries. Zero re-training required post-launch.
Section 10
What I'd
do differently
"I spent too long designing for the reviewer and not long enough watching the submitters. Reviewers could articulate their needs. Submitters couldn't — I had to watch them work. I should have started there."

The bounce-back problem was almost entirely a submitter comprehension problem, not a reviewer workflow problem. The form had fields like "Select Business Impact" with no guidance on what that meant in commodity trading context. Submitters guessed. Reviewers rejected. A cloze test on the form labels in week one would have surfaced this before I spent three weeks mapping the reviewer workflow.

I also underestimated the email notification problem. Status change emails went out with the subject line "INC-0034 status changed" — no context, no next action. Multiple submitters told me they ignored these emails because they looked like system spam. The in-app notification strip was added in a later sprint. It should have been designed alongside the email in the same sprint.

What I'd defend completely: the fight to embed comments in the form itself. Three stakeholders pushed for a simpler rejection email. I showed the support ticket data, held the position, and it became the feature users mention first in post-launch feedback. The data was the argument. The data won.
